entry: Development of the idea that [[Matter|matter]] is composed of indivisible particles, from ancient philosophy to modern physics. The word atom comes from the Greek atomos, meaning indivisible, but ancient atomism rested on philosophical reasoning rather than experiment. Working in the late 17th century, [[Robert Boyle]] developed the concept of a chemical element, and [[Antoine Lavoisier]] later showed that compounds consist of elements in constant proportion, also defining the [[Conservation of mass|law of conservation of mass]]. In 1804 [[John Dalton]] noticed that the amounts of one element combining with a fixed amount of another differ by ratios of small whole numbers, which he took as evidence that elements combine by basic units of weight. [[Richard Feynman]] described the atomic hypothesis as the single most prolific scientific concept. Physicists later found that atoms have an internal structure and can be divided.

Development of human flight from early kites and glider experiments to jet-powered air travel. Kite flying in China, several hundred years BC, is considered the earliest example of man-made flight. In the 15th century [[Leonardo da Vinci]] designed flying machines, but they were unworkable with contemporary knowledge. The [[Montgolfier brothers]] invented the hot-air balloon in the late 18th century, and balloons were used for military purposes from the end of that century, with France establishing balloon companies during the French Revolution. In 1903 the [[Wright brothers]] flew the first airplane. Rigid steerable balloons pioneered by Ferdinand von Zeppelin, known as [[Airship|airships]], dominated long-distance flight until the 1930s, when large flying boats became popular for trans-oceanic routes. After World War II, airplanes operating from land, powered first by propellers and then by jet engines, reshaped both civil and military aviation.

Development of the study of the living world, from ancient medicine and natural history to modern molecular research. The biological sciences emerged from traditions of medicine and natural history reaching back to Ayurveda, ancient Egyptian medicine and the works of [[Aristotle]] and [[Galen]]. During the Renaissance, [[Andreas Vesalius]] and [[William Harvey]] used experimentation and careful observation in physiology, and [[Antonie van Leeuwenhoek]] revealed the world of microorganisms by microscopy, laying the groundwork for cell theory. [[Charles Darwin]] synthesized these developments, along with embryology and paleontology, into a theory of evolution by natural selection. In the early 20th century the rediscovery of the work of [[Gregor Mendel]] led to rapid development of genetics. After Watson and Crick proposed the structure of [[DNA]], biology was largely split between organismal biology and the cellular and molecular fields.

Development of the study and transformation of matter, from prehistoric crafts to modern science. By 1000 BC civilizations used technologies that formed the basis of later branches of chemistry, including the discovery of fire, the extraction of metals from ores, making pottery and glazes, fermenting beer and wine, and making glass and [[Alloy|alloys]] such as bronze. Gold seems to have been the earliest metal used by humans, and tin, lead and copper could be recovered from their ores by heating. Combining copper and tin produced bronze, a major shift that began the [[Bronze Age]] about 3500 BC. [[Alchemy]], the protoscience of chemistry, did not explain the nature of matter, but its experiments set the stage for modern chemistry. In the 17th century [[Robert Boyle]] pursued experimentation over alchemical jargon, and in the 18th century [[Antoine Lavoisier]] helped establish the law of conservation of mass.

Development of human methods for transmitting information, from early symbols and speech to digital networks. Human communication began with the origin of speech, circa 100,000 BCE. The oldest known cave painting, in Chauvet Cave, dates to around 30,000 BCE, and [[Cave painting|cave paintings]] were among the earliest communicative symbols. Writing developed in Mesopotamia around 3200 BCE, when proto-writing evolved into [[Cuneiform]] script on clay tablets. The movable-type printing press invented by [[Johannes Gutenberg]] circa 1440 CE scaled text reproduction and fostered wider literacy. In the 19th century [[Samuel Morse]]'s telegraph, operational from 1844, sent coded messages over wires, and [[Alexander Graham Bell]]'s 1876 telephone patent introduced voice transmission. Wireless broadcasting followed in the 20th century, and packet-switching networks such as [[ARPANET]] appeared in 1969. The [[World Wide Web]] proposal of 1989 integrated hypertext for public internet use by 1991.

Development of devices for calculation and data processing, from ancient counting aids to modern microprocessors. The [[Abacus]] was used for arithmetic in Babylonia as early as c. 2700–2300 BC, and the [[Antikythera mechanism]] was an analog device for astronomical calculation. [[Charles Babbage]] planned an Analytical Engine in the 1830s that introduced concepts of a central processing unit and memory, but it was never fully constructed. [[Konrad Zuse]]'s Z3 (1941) was the first functional programmable digital computer. [[Vacuum tube|Vacuum tubes]] and then [[Transistor|transistors]] replaced earlier machines, and the [[Integrated circuit]] followed. The microprocessor enabled the miniaturized [[Personal computer|personal computer]] in the 1970s. Intel's 4004 had 2,300 transistors, and the Apple II, designed by Steve Wozniak, popularized home computing. Modern hardware includes multi-core CPUs and GPUs for parallel processing.

Development of dance from prehistoric ritual and social activity to theatrical and cinematic forms. Dance leaves few durable physical artifacts, so the point at which it became part of human culture is difficult to determine. Prehistoric traces include rock paintings at Bhimbetka in India and an Egyptian tomb depicting dancing figures from c. 3300 BC. Dance has been part of ceremony, ritual and celebration, and it was used in healing rituals from the [[Brazil|Brazilian]] rainforest to the [[Kalahari Desert]]. Dance was also an early means of expression, used to perform myths and to convey feelings. In 17th-century France the codification of [[Ballet]] technique took place under the patronage of [[Louis XIV]]. In the 20th century [[Isadora Duncan]]'s free-form expressionism challenged classical rigidity, and later forms drew on traditions such as jazz and hip-hop.

Development of ideas about wealth, property, trade and the economy, from ancient philosophy to modern schools of economics. In the Western world economics was part of philosophy until the 18th–19th century Industrial Revolution. [[Hesiod]] wrote the earliest known work on the basic origins of economic thought, and [[Aristotle]] examined the art of wealth acquisition and questioned whether property is best left in private or public hands. In India the [[Arthashastra]], traditionally attributed to [[Chanakya]] of the Maurya Empire, treated economic policy within a treatise on statecraft. [[Thomas Aquinas]] argued that businesses had a moral obligation to sell goods at a just price. [[Adam Smith]]'s *Wealth of Nations* (1776) championed division of labor and free markets. In the 20th century [[John Maynard Keynes]] advocated active fiscal policy, while [[Friedrich Hayek]] emphasized knowledge dispersion and spontaneous order.

Development of motion pictures from 19th-century optical entertainments to digital production. Precursors included shadow puppetry, the [[Camera obscura|camera obscura]] and the magic lantern. In 1833 scientific study of a stroboscopic illusion by Joseph Plateau, [[Michael Faraday]] and Simon Stampfer led to the Fantascope, also known as the phenakistiscope. The [[Lumière brothers]] screened short films to a paying audience in Paris on 28 December 1895, generally regarded as the breakthrough of projected motion pictures. The earliest films were black and white, under a minute long and without recorded sound. Film grew from a novelty into a mass entertainment industry with studios throughout the world. Television from the 1950s, home video from the 1980s and the internet from the 1990s influenced how films were distributed and watched. Digital production spread in the 1990s, leading to realistic visual effects and feature-length [[Computer animation|computer animations]].

Development of games from prehistoric [[Dice|dice]] and knucklebones to modern sports and computer simulations. Games are an integral part of all cultures and among the oldest forms of human social interaction, typically featuring agreed rules, competition and elements of chance. Games transmitted cultural worldviews, served as markers of social status, and taught spiritual and ethical lessons. Dice were invented at least 5,000 years ago. [[Board game|Board games]] probably originated in the ancient Near East, and 49 small carved figures found at the 5,000-year-old Başur Höyük burial mound in southeast [[Turkey]] may be the earliest gaming pieces found. Senet, found in predynastic and First Dynasty burial sites in [[Egypt]], was played on a board of 30 squares and reflected the journey of the soul in the afterlife. In India, chaturanga, a precursor to [[Chess]], emerged around the 6th century CE.

Development of the study and mapping of the Earth, from ancient Mesopotamian maps to an academic discipline. The word geography, from the Greek for Earth-writing, was first used by [[Eratosthenes]], but recognizable practices such as [[Cartography|cartography]] existed earlier. The oldest known world maps date to ancient [[Babylon]], and the best-known Babylonian map, the Imago Mundi of 600 BC, shows Babylon on the Euphrates surrounded by a circular landmass. The Greeks viewed [[Homer]] as the founder of geography, since the *Iliad* and *Odyssey* contain much geographical information. [[Thales of Miletus]] laid down astronomical and mathematical rules that allowed geography to be studied scientifically, and his successor Anaximander attempted the first scale map of the known world. [[Herodotus]]' *Histories* describes much of the known world, including Egypt, Scythia and Persia. Geography later became a distinct academic discipline.

Development of the natural science of geology, from ancient observations of fossils and minerals to plate tectonics. In the 4th century BC [[Aristotle]] observed the slow rate of geological change, and his successor Theophrastus described many minerals and ores in *On Stones*. [[Pliny the Elder]] was among the first to identify amber as fossilized tree resin and laid the basis of crystallography by recognizing the octahedral habit of diamond. [[Al-Biruni|Abu al-Rayhan al-Biruni]] wrote the earliest writings on the geology of India, hypothesizing that the Indian subcontinent was once a sea. [[Shen Kuo]] formulated a theory of geomorphology based on marine fossils found in mountains hundreds of miles from the Pacific Ocean. In the 18th and 19th centuries [[James Hutton]] introduced uniformitarianism, which [[Charles Lyell]] later expanded. In 1912 [[Alfred Wegener]] proposed continental drift, which laid groundwork for [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonics]].

Study of sexual behavior, its regulation and its social and political impact from prehistory to the present. Sexual speech has been subject to varying standards of decorum, and writing was used by only a small part of most societies, leaving little explicit evidence. In his 1861 book *Mother Right*, Johann Bachofen argued that human sexuality began as sex-positive and passed through matriarchal and then patriarchal stages, a view drawn almost entirely from ancient mythology. [[Friedrich Engels]] and Lewis Henry Morgan were influenced by Bachofen but criticized his ideas. Modern explanations are based in evolutionary biology and human behavioral ecology, which hold that current behavior reflects selective forces in the Pleistocene. Among Native American tribes, the berdache, a cross-gender role, existed in several groups before colonial times. The term is now considered outdated and is often replaced by two spirit, which emphasizes how Native Americans themselves viewed these individuals.

Development of the scientific study of language, from Mesopotamian word lists to modern subfields. Language use was first systematically documented in [[Mesopotamia]], where lexical lists from the 3rd to the 2nd millennia BCE (3000 to 1000 BCE) offered glossaries of Sumerian and phonetic vocabularies of foreign languages. In ancient India, [[Pāṇini]] systematically described [[Sanskrit]], and [[Aristotle]] laid the foundation of Western linguistics as part of the study of rhetoric. Modern approaches developed in the 18th century. In the early 20th century [[Ferdinand de Saussure]] established linguistics as an autonomous discipline within the social sciences, treating language as a semiotic system with subfields of phonology, morphology, syntax and semantics. [[Noam Chomsky]]'s generative grammar, published in 1957, shifted focus to cognitive mechanisms. Today linguistics includes applied, psycholinguistic, neurolinguistic, [[Sociolinguistics|sociolinguistic]] and computational subfields.

Development of the application of pigments to surfaces, from [[Paleolithic]] cave art to modern abstraction. Cave paintings in Leang Karampuang, [[Sulawesi]], were dated in a study published in *Nature* in 2024 to approximately 51,200 years old. In Paleolithic times animals were the most common subjects, including the rhinoceros and large Felidae in Chauvet Cave, painted around 31,000 BC. Ancient civilizations used mineral pigments on walls and portable media, as in Egyptian tomb frescoes and Chinese Han dynasty lacquerware. Greek and Roman artists advanced linear perspective, and in the [[Renaissance]] oil binders enabled layered glazing and chiaroscuro, as pioneered by [[Jan van Eyck]]. Romantic painters such as Francisco de Goya, [[John Constable]] and [[J. M. W. Turner]] gave expression to the idea of art for art's sake. Until the early 20th century painting relied mainly on representational motifs, after which [[Abstraction|abstract]] approaches gained favor.

Development of the study of matter and energy, from ancient natural philosophy to quantum theory and cosmology. [[Thales of Miletus]] proposed that every event had a natural cause, and [[Democritus]] and Leucippus formulated early atomism. [[Archimedes]] advanced statics and hydrostatics, formulating the principle of buoyancy. In the Middle Ages [[Ibn al-Haytham]] pioneered experimental optics. The Scientific Revolution of the 17th century, including the discovery of the law of gravity, began physics as an experimental science. [[Isaac Newton]]'s *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica* established classical mechanics and universal gravitation. In the 19th century [[James Clerk Maxwell]] unified electricity and magnetism. At the start of the 20th century, [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]], relativity and atomic theory transformed the field, as [[Albert Einstein]]'s special relativity revealed time dilation and general relativity described gravity as spacetime curvature.

Development of human thought about government, authority, justice and the organization of society, from ancient China and Greece to modern ideologies. Many histories of Western political thought trace its origins to ancient Greece, where [[Socrates]], [[Plato]] and [[Aristotle]] are traditionally treated as especially influential. Non-Western traditions are also significant. In China the Hundred Schools of Thought included [[Confucius]], whose ideas of moral example and hierarchical order were influential, and [[Legalism (Chinese philosophy)|Legalism]], which argued that authoritarian discipline was crucial for governing. Legalism was dominant under the Qin dynasty, and State Confucianism replaced it in the Han dynasty. In ancient India the [[Arthashastra]] is an early treatise on governance and politics. Islamic political philosophy expanded rapidly from the 7th century. Medieval and modern thinkers, including [[Thomas Aquinas]], John Locke and Karl Marx, developed influential theories.

Development of the scientific study of behavior and mental processes, from ancient philosophy of the soul to cognitive science. Philosophical interest in the human mind dates back to ancient civilizations, and [[Aristotle]]'s *De Anima* treated the soul as the principle of life. Experimental psychology began in 1854 in [[Leipzig]], when Gustav Fechner created the first theory of how judgments about sensory experiences are made. In 1879 [[Wilhelm Wundt]] founded the first psychological laboratory dedicated exclusively to psychological research. [[Sigmund Freud]] independently developed psychoanalysis in Vienna. In the 20th century [[John B. Watson]] formulated behaviorism, which [[B. F. Skinner]] popularized through operant conditioning. From the 1930s a humanistic approach led by [[Carl Rogers]] and [[Abraham Maslow]] emphasized self-actualization. The final decades of the 20th century brought cognitive science, which draws on cognitive psychology, linguistics, computer science and neurobiology.

Development of the institution of owning human beings as property, from ancient [[Mesopotamia]] to the present. Slavery was institutionalized by the time the first civilizations emerged, and it features in the [[Code of Hammurabi]], which refers to it as an established institution. Agriculture after the [[Neolithic Revolution]] offered greater opportunity for mass chattel slavery. Islamic slavery encompassed much of Western and Central Asia, Northern and Eastern Africa, India and Europe from the 7th to the 20th century. Beginning in the 16th century, European merchants, starting mainly with merchants from [[Portugal]], initiated the [[Atlantic slave trade]], mostly purchasing captives from [[West Africa]] kingdoms and transporting them to colonies in the [[Americas]]. The transatlantic trade was eventually curtailed after European and American governments passed legislation abolishing their nations' involvement. In 2019 an estimated 40.3 million people worldwide were subject to some form of slavery, and [[Human trafficking]] remains an international problem.

Development of sociology as a systematic study of society, from Enlightenment thought to the modern social sciences. Sociology emerged primarily out of Enlightenment thought as a positivist science of society shortly after the French Revolution, in reaction to modernity, capitalism, urbanization and imperialism. [[Auguste Comte]] coined the term in 1838. Sociological perspectives can be found in the thought of ancient writers such as [[Herodotus]], [[Thucydides]] and [[Plato]], and of non-European thinkers such as [[Confucius]]. In the late 19th century sociology took particular interest in the emergence of the modern nation state, including its institutions, units of socialization and means of surveillance. [[Karl Marx]], Herbert Spencer and [[Max Weber]] developed influential approaches, and the first sociology department was established at the [[University of Chicago]] in 1892. Quantitative social research techniques are now common tools for governments and businesses.

Development of human and artificial flight beyond Earth's atmosphere, from early rocketry to commercial spaceflight. Spaceflight became an engineering possibility with [[Robert H. Goddard]]'s 1919 paper on liquid-fuel rockets, which influenced [[Wernher von Braun]]. The first rocket to reach space was the German [[V-2 rocket]], on a vertical test flight in June 1944. The Soviet Union launched [[Sputnik 1]] in 1957 and later sent [[Yuri Gagarin]], the first human in space, into orbit in 1961. The United States landed the first men on the Moon in 1969 with [[Apollo 11]]. Long-duration habitation followed with space stations such as Mir and the [[International Space Station]], which has been continuously occupied since 2000. In 2020 [[SpaceX]] became the first commercial operator to launch a crewed mission to the ISS.

Development of organized physical competition from prehistoric activity to modern professional sport. Sport had early links with warfare and entertainment, and competition was used to determine whether individuals were fit for military service. Cave paintings in France appear to depict sprinting in the Upper Paleolithic, and rock art in Egypt shows swimming and archery. Wrestlers are depicted on Sumerian stone slabs dated to around 3000 BC, and the [[Epic of Gilgamesh]] describes belt wrestling. Monuments at Beni Hasan dating to around 2000 BC show that wrestling, weightlifting, long jump, swimming and archery were well developed in [[Ancient Egypt]]. The first Olympic Games were recorded in 776 BC at Olympia, where they were held every four years until 393 AD. [[Pierre de Coubertin]]'s 1896 Olympic revival transformed sport into a global arena. In the 19th century [[Cricket]] and [[Association football]] gained standardized rules, enabling mass participation and commercialization.

Human history of the islands of Great Britain and Ireland, from early habitation to the modern states of the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland. The islands were inhabited sporadically from around 900,000 years ago, with stone tools and footprints found near Happisburgh in Norfolk, England. [[Neanderthal|Neanderthals]] inhabited Britain intermittently until around 50–40,000 years ago. Around 4000 BC migrants from central Europe began the [[Neolithic Revolution]] in the islands, adopting agriculture and sedentary living, and undertook mass [[Deforestation|deforestation]]. The British Isles were linked to continental Europe by a territory named [[Doggerland]] until it was submerged. England and Scotland were sovereign kingdoms until 1603, when they came under one monarch, and united as one kingdom in 1707. The British monarch was [[Head of state|head of state]] of all the countries of the islands from 1603 until the enactment of the [[Republic of Ireland]] Act in 1949.

Regional history of the Caribbean islands, from [[Indigenous peoples|Indigenous]] settlement and European colonization to independence. Trinidad was the first Caribbean island settled, as early as 9000/8000 BCE, and it was the only island that could have been colonized by Indigenous people from the South American mainland without crossing open sea. In 1492 [[Christopher Columbus]] landed in the Caribbean and claimed the region for Spain. From the 1620s and 1630s non-Hispanic privateers, traders and settlers established permanent colonies on islands neglected by Spain, including [[Jamaica]] and [[Martinique]]. Enslaved Africans were brought through the [[Atlantic slave trade]] to replace depleted native labor, and the [[Haitian Revolution]] dismantled French slavery in Saint-Domingue. After the [[Spanish–American War]] in 1898, Cuba and Puerto Rico were no longer part of the [[Spanish Empire]]. Many islands have attained independence, while others have formal political ties with major powers, including the United States.

headword: History of the Democratic Republic of the Congo
sort_key: history of the democratic republic of the congo
entry: Political history of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, from early states to the present. The [[Kingdom of Kongo]] controlled much of western and central Africa between the 14th and early 19th centuries. Along a coastal strip about 400 kilometres (250 mi) long, about 4 million people were enslaved and sent across the Atlantic in the [[Atlantic slave trade]]. From 1879 [[Leopold II of Belgium]] sent agents to establish posts along the Congo River, and he claimed the [[Congo Free State]] in 1885. Belgium granted independence in 1960, followed by the Congo Crisis.Colonel [[Mobutu Sese Seko|Joseph Mobutu]] seized power in 1965 and renamed the country [[Zaire]]. Laurent-Désiré Kabila took power in 1997 and renamed the country the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and the [[Second Congo War]] followed, in which millions were killed or displaced. In 2018 Félix Tshisekedi was elected president, in the first peaceful transfer of power since independence.
